topic_description: graph clustered federated learning for non-IID graph classification using dynamic time warping
idea_name: Graph-Aware Dynamic Time Warping for Federated Learning

raw_idea.Problem: Existing federated learning approaches for graph classification struggle with non-IID graph data across clients, especially when the graph structures and temporal dynamics vary significantly.
raw_idea.Existing Methods: Current methods typically use graph neural networks (GNNs) with federated averaging, but fail to capture complex temporal dependencies in dynamic graphs.
raw_idea.Motivation: Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) has shown promise in aligning temporal sequences, but has not been effectively integrated into federated graph learning frameworks. Combining DTW with graph-aware federated learning could better handle non-IID graph data with varying temporal dynamics.
raw_idea.Proposed Method: We propose Graph-DTW-Fed, a novel federated learning framework for non-IID graph classification. The key ideas are: 1) A graph-aware DTW layer that aligns temporal graph sequences across clients before aggregation. 2) A hierarchical attention mechanism that learns to focus on important nodes, edges, and time steps when performing DTW. 3) A federated optimization strategy that alternates between local graph DTW updates and global model aggregation. 4) A clustering module that groups clients with similar graph dynamics to enable more effective knowledge transfer. The local models use graph neural networks augmented with our graph-DTW layers. During training, clients perform local updates using their private graph data. The server then clusters clients and performs aggregation within each cluster using our hierarchical attention mechanism. This process is repeated for multiple rounds to obtain a global model that can generalize across diverse graph distributions.
raw_idea.Experiment Plan: We will evaluate on multiple dynamic graph classification benchmarks like DYNGRAPH2VEC and JODIE, comparing against federated GNN baselines. Key metrics include classification accuracy, F1 score, and communication efficiency. We will also analyze how performance varies with graph structural differences and temporal misalignment between clients.

full_experiment_plan.Title: Graph-DTW-Fed: A Federated Learning Framework for Non-IID Graph Classification with Dynamic Time Warping
full_experiment_plan.Problem Statement: Existing federated learning approaches for graph classification struggle with non-IID graph data across clients, especially when the graph structures and temporal dynamics vary significantly. This challenge hinders the effective collaboration of distributed clients in learning a global model for graph classification tasks.
full_experiment_plan.Motivation: Current federated learning methods for graph classification typically use graph neural networks (GNNs) with federated averaging, but fail to capture complex temporal dependencies in dynamic graphs. Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) has shown promise in aligning temporal sequences but has not been effectively integrated into federated graph learning frameworks. Combining DTW with graph-aware federated learning could better handle non-IID graph data with varying temporal dynamics, leading to improved performance and generalization across diverse graph distributions.
full_experiment_plan.Proposed Method: We propose Graph-DTW-Fed, a novel federated learning framework for non-IID graph classification. The key components are: 1) A graph-aware DTW layer that aligns temporal graph sequences across clients before aggregation. 2) A hierarchical attention mechanism that learns to focus on important nodes, edges, and time steps when performing DTW. 3) A federated optimization strategy that alternates between local graph DTW updates and global model aggregation. 4) A clustering module that groups clients with similar graph dynamics to enable more effective knowledge transfer. The local models use graph neural networks augmented with our graph-DTW layers. During training, clients perform local updates using their private graph data. The server then clusters clients and performs aggregation within each cluster using our hierarchical attention mechanism.

Step-by-Step Experiment Plan.Step 1: Data Preparation: Use DYNGRAPH2VEC and JODIE datasets for dynamic graph classification. Preprocess the data to create non-IID distributions across simulated clients by varying temporal dynamics and graph structures.
Step-by-Step Experiment Plan.Step 2: Model Implementation: Implement the Graph-DTW-Fed model using PyTorch Geometric for graph neural networks and tslearn for DTW operations. The model should include: (a) A graph neural network backbone (e.g., GCN or GAT), (b) A graph-aware DTW layer, (c) A hierarchical attention mechanism, and (d) A clustering module.
Step-by-Step Experiment Plan.Step 3: Federated Learning Setup: Implement the federated learning framework using PySyft or FedML libraries. Set up a central server and multiple client nodes. Implement the federated optimization strategy that alternates between local updates and global aggregation.
Step-by-Step Experiment Plan.Step 4: Baseline Implementation: Implement baseline methods for comparison: (a) Federated GNN with FedAvg, (b) Centralized GNN, (c) Local GNN training without federation.
Step-by-Step Experiment Plan.Step 5: Hyperparameter Tuning: Perform grid search for key hyperparameters: learning rate, number of GNN layers, DTW window size, number of client clusters, and local update steps per round.
Step-by-Step Experiment Plan.Step 6: Training and Evaluation: Train the Graph-DTW-Fed model and baselines for multiple federated rounds. Evaluate performance using classification accuracy, F1 score, and communication efficiency (measured by the number of rounds to convergence).
Step-by-Step Experiment Plan.Step 7: Ablation Studies: Conduct ablation studies to analyze the impact of each component: (a) Graph-DTW layer, (b) Hierarchical attention mechanism, (c) Client clustering.
Step-by-Step Experiment Plan.Step 8: Non-IID Analysis: Analyze how performance varies with different levels of graph structural differences and temporal misalignment between clients.
Step-by-Step Experiment Plan.Step 9: Visualization: Create visualizations of learned DTW alignments and attention weights to provide insights into the model's behavior.
Step-by-Step Experiment Plan.Step 10: Results Compilation and Analysi: Compile all results, generate plots, and perform statistical tests to compare Graph-DTW-Fed with baselines.

Test Case Examples.Explanation: Graph-DTW-Fed outperforms the baseline by better aligning temporal sequences across clients and focusing on important graph elements, leading to improved accuracy, F1 score, and faster convergence.

full_experiment_plan.Fallback Plan: If Graph-DTW-Fed does not significantly outperform baselines, we can pivot the project to an in-depth analysis of why DTW and hierarchical attention do not improve federated graph learning as expected. We can investigate the learned DTW alignments and attention weights to understand if they are capturing meaningful patterns. Additionally, we can explore alternative time series alignment techniques or graph representation methods that might be more suitable for federated learning scenarios. Another direction could be to analyze how different types of non-IID distributions affect federated graph learning performance, which could provide valuable insights for future research in this area.
